rounds.proof_sketch: block_dim changes from 256 to 1. Original: stride=256 means each thread processes ~1 element. Mutated: stride=1 means thread 0 processes ALL 256 elements in reduction. With 8 outer loop iterations (base=0,32,64,...,224) and 32 inner iterations each, thread 0 multiplies all elements while other threads overlap.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the loop stride from blockDim.x=256 to blockDim.y=1. This fundamentally alters which elements each thread processes. In the original, with reduction_size=256 and stride=256, thread i processes only element i. In the mutant, stride=1 causes thread 0 to process all 256 elements, and other threads process overlapping subsets. The warp reduction then multiplies these incorrect partial products together, yielding wildly different results for any non-trivial input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Use values slightly different from 1.0 (e.g., 1.1 or 0.9) so that the exponential difference in multiplication count produces clearly divergent results. Values near 1.0 minimize overflow while maximizing relative error detection.
rounds.recommendations: When using thread block dimension variables in loop strides, add compile-time or runtime assertions that verify the expected launch configuration. Consider using explicit named constants instead of relying on blockDim values that depend on launch configuration.
rounds.suggested_code:
def generate_inputs(device):
    # Use constant 1.1 - original gives 1.1^256, mutant gives vastly different result
    # due to stride bug causing overlapping element processing
    x = torch.full((16, 256, 256), 1.1, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    return [x]
